title: Японцы отказались от рыбы  (The Japanese Refuse the Fish)

segments.t: Waiters carry all the fish dishes back to the kitchen because the Japanese delegation immediately smelled that the fish wasn't fresh. Mikhail Jekovich deducts the cost from the cooks' wages, and Senya stubbornly eats a piece to prove them wrong.
Потому что она совсем не свежая.
Стоимость блюд я вычту у вас.
Не надо моих гостей кормить этим.
Now let's go back through their conversation line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
'The waiters are carrying your fish back.' Focusing on the waiters on the spot, Fedya centers the thought on "ofitsianty" ("waiters", from "ofitsiant") without wasting a word.
'The Japanese refused to eat this fish.' Focusing on the man on the spot, Mikhail chooses "yapontsy" ("Japanese man", from the root "yaponets") so Fedya hears the exact meaning.
Потому что она совсем не свежая.
'Because it is not fresh at all.' Mikhail speaks up steadily around Fedya, leaving no doubt about where he stands.
Стоимость блюд я вычту у вас.
'I will deduct the cost of the dishes from you.' Touching on the cost beside Fedya, Mikhail brings in "stoimost" ("to cost") to make the meaning unmistakable.
'Wow, that is quite a fine.' Checking on a fine at once, Fedya links the Russian words directly in the present with no word for "am", "is", or "are" needed.
Не надо моих гостей кормить этим.
'Do not feed my guests with this.' Talking about his guests toward Fedya, Mikhail lets Fedya see exactly where things stand.
'By the way, this is very tasty fish.' Underscoring how tasty things are around Mikhail, Senya leans on "vkusnaya" ("tasty", a form of "vkusnyy") to give the remark its edge.
'The Japanese simply do not understand anything.' Touching on the man beside Fedya, Senya uses the little word "prosto" ("simply, just") to make the point sound effortless.
'Well, how do you like our fish?' Fedya tests briskly why things suddenly took this turn between them.
'The discounted fish went down well!' Addressing the discount on the spot, Senya chooses "skidkoy" ("discount", from the root "skidka") so Fedya hears the exact meaning.
'Senya, what is wrong with you right now?' Cutting in dryly right here, Fedya links the Russian words directly in the present with no word for "am", "is", or "are" needed.
'I need to step out urgently for a minute.' Senya replies promptly toward Fedya, steering the talk right where he wants it.
Потому что она совсем не свежая.
Стоимость блюд я вычту у вас.
Не надо моих гостей кормить этим.
Senya's stomach immediately rebels against the bargain fish, while Mikhail sneaks his pony inside the hotel for the night. Until next time!
